Distinguer convergence et divergence ; calculer une limite ; utiliser comparaison, gendarmes et convergence monotone.
Distinguish convergence from divergence; compute a limit; use comparison, the squeeze theorem and monotone convergence.

\(u_n\to\ell\in\R\) signifie que tout intervalle ouvert contenant \(\ell\) contient tous les termes à partir d'un certain rang. On dit que \((u_n)\) converge vers \(\ell\).
\(u_n\to+\infty\) signifie que pour tout réel \(A\), il existe un rang \(N\) tel que \(n\ge N\Rightarrow u_n\ge A\). \(u_n\to-\infty\) signifie que pour tout réel \(A\), il existe \(N\) tel que \(n\ge N\Rightarrow u_n\le A\).

\(u_n\to\ell\in\R\) means that every open interval containing \(\ell\) contains all the terms from some index onwards. We say that \((u_n)\) converges to \(\ell\).
\(u_n\to+\infty\) means that for every real number \(A\), there is an index \(N\) such that \(n\ge N\Rightarrow u_n\ge A\). \(u_n\to-\infty\) means that for every real number \(A\), there is \(N\) such that \(n\ge N\Rightarrow u_n\le A\).
Une suite peut n'avoir aucune limite, même infinie : \((-1)^n\) oscille entre \(-1\) et \(1\). Toute suite convergente est bornée, mais la réciproque est fausse.
A sequence may have no limit at all, not even an infinite one: \((-1)^n\) oscillates between \(-1\) and \(1\). Every convergent sequence is bounded, but the converse is false.

Pour deux suites convergentes de limites \(a,b\), la somme tend vers \(a+b\), le produit vers \(ab\) et le quotient vers \(\frac{a}{b}\) si \(b\ne0\). Les règles avec l'infini s'utilisent en contrôlant les signes. Les formes \(+\infty-\infty\), \(0\times\infty\), \(\frac{\infty}{\infty}\), \(\frac{0}{0}\) ne permettent pas de conclure directement.

For two convergent sequences with limits \(a,b\), the sum tends to \(a+b\), the product to \(ab\) and the quotient to \(\frac{a}{b}\) if \(b\ne0\). The rules involving infinity are used by keeping track of the signs. The forms \(+\infty-\infty\), \(0\times\infty\), \(\frac{\infty}{\infty}\), \(\frac{0}{0}\) do not allow a direct conclusion.

\(\frac{3n^2-n+1}{2n^2+4}=\frac{3-\frac{1}{n}+\frac{1}{n^2}}{2+\frac{4}{n^2}}\to\frac{3}{2}\). Pour \(\sqrt{n^2+n}-n\), multiplier par la quantité conjuguée donne \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{n}}+1}\to\frac{1}{2}\).

\(\frac{3n^2-n+1}{2n^2+4}=\frac{3-\frac{1}{n}+\frac{1}{n^2}}{2+\frac{4}{n^2}}\to\frac{3}{2}\). For \(\sqrt{n^2+n}-n\), multiplying by the conjugate expression gives \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{n}}+1}\to\frac{1}{2}\).

Si \(u_n\le v_n\) à partir d'un certain rang et \(u_n\to+\infty\), alors \(v_n\to+\infty\). Si \(a_n\le u_n\le b_n\) à partir d'un certain rang et \(a_n,b_n\to\ell\), alors \(u_n\to\ell\) (gendarmes).
Toute suite croissante et majorée converge. Toute suite décroissante et minorée converge. Ce théorème est admis.

If \(u_n\le v_n\) from some index onwards and \(u_n\to+\infty\), then \(v_n\to+\infty\). If \(a_n\le u_n\le b_n\) from some index onwards and \(a_n,b_n\to\ell\), then \(u_n\to\ell\) (squeeze theorem).
Every increasing sequence that is bounded above converges. Every decreasing sequence that is bounded below converges. This theorem is admitted (taken without proof).
Pour tout \(A\), les termes de \(u\) dépassent \(A\) au-delà d'un rang \(N_1\). L'inégalité \(v_n\ge u_n\) vaut au-delà d'un rang \(N_2\). Pour \(n\ge\max(N_1,N_2)\), \(v_n\ge A\).
For every \(A\), the terms of \(u\) exceed \(A\) beyond an index \(N_1\). The inequality \(v_n\ge u_n\) holds beyond an index \(N_2\). For \(n\ge\max(N_1,N_2)\), \(v_n\ge A\).
Pour tout \(A\), la non-majoration fournit \(N\) tel que \(u_N>A\). Par croissance, \(n\ge N\Rightarrow u_n\ge u_N>A\), d'où \(u_n\to+\infty\). La non-majoration seule ne suffit pas.

For every \(A\), the fact that the sequence is not bounded above provides \(N\) such that \(u_N>A\). Since the sequence is increasing, \(n\ge N\Rightarrow u_n\ge u_N>A\), hence \(u_n\to+\infty\). Not being bounded above is not enough on its own.

\[q^n\longrightarrow\begin{cases}0&\text{si }-1<q<1,\\1&\text{si }q=1,\\+\infty&\text{si }q>1.\end{cases}\]
Si \(q\le-1\), \((q^n)\) n'a pas de limite : alternance pour \(q=-1\) ; sous-suites paire et impaire de signes opposés et de modules non bornés pour \(q<-1\).

\[q^n\longrightarrow\begin{cases}0&\text{si }-1<q<1,\\1&\text{si }q=1,\\+\infty&\text{si }q>1.\end{cases}\]
If \(q\le-1\), \((q^n)\) has no limit: alternation for \(q=-1\); for \(q<-1\), the even and odd subsequences have opposite signs and unbounded moduli.

Fixons \(a\ge0\). Démontrons \(P(n)\) : « \((1+a)^n\ge1+na\) ». Au rang \(0\), les deux membres valent \(1\).
Fixons \(n\ge0\) et supposons \(P(n)\) vraie. Comme \(1+a>0\),
\[(1+a)^{n+1}\ge(1+na)(1+a)=1+(n+1)a+na^2\ge1+(n+1)a.\]
C'est \(P(n+1)\) car \(na^2\ge0\). Par récurrence, l'inégalité est vraie pour tout \(n\ge0\). Si \(q>1\), prendre \(a=q-1>0\) et comparer à \(1+na\). Si \(0<q<1\), appliquer ce résultat à \(\frac{1}{q}\), puis prendre les inverses. Pour \(-1<q<0\), \(|q^n|=|q|^n\to0\) et les gendarmes concluent. Le cas \(q=0\) se traite à partir du rang \(1\).

Fix \(a\ge0\). Let us prove \(P(n)\): "\((1+a)^n\ge1+na\)". At index \(0\), both sides equal \(1\).
Fix \(n\ge0\) and assume \(P(n)\) is true. Since \(1+a>0\),
\[(1+a)^{n+1}\ge(1+na)(1+a)=1+(n+1)a+na^2\ge1+(n+1)a.\]
This is \(P(n+1)\) because \(na^2\ge0\). By induction, the inequality holds for every \(n\ge0\). If \(q>1\), take \(a=q-1>0\) and compare with \(1+na\). If \(0<q<1\), apply this result to \(\frac{1}{q}\), then take reciprocals. For \(-1<q<0\), \(|q^n|=|q|^n\to0\) and the squeeze theorem concludes. The case \(q=0\) is handled from index \(1\) onwards.

A limit is not a last term — 30 min.

Consider the sequence \((u_n)\) defined on \(\N\) by \(u_n=2+\frac3{n+1}\).
  1. Compute \(u_0\), \(u_9\) and \(u_{99}\). Is there an integer \(n\) such that \(u_n=2\)? Justify.
  2. Find the smallest integer \(N\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge N\), \(|u_n-2|<0.01\).
  3. Let \(\varepsilon>0\). Give, in terms of \(\varepsilon\), an integer \(N\) such that \(|u_n-2|<\varepsilon\) for every \(n\ge N\).
  4. Define on \(\N\) the sequence \((v_n)\) by \(v_n=2+\frac{(-1)^n}{n+1}\). Prove that it converges to \(2\) and that it is not monotonic. What does this example show?
